name: Tanaina
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: There is no distinctive tone of any kind in Tanaina. (This is also true of Eyak, Ahtena, Upper Kuskokwim, Hupa, and many other Athapaskan languages, especially those which have retained stem-final glottalization where that was present in PA.) The intonation pattern of Tanaina does include a simple form of word-stress, however. The general rule is stress on the penult, regardless of morphological structure or vowel-grade: łnazéldaq 'I'm asleep', łnazíldaq 'you're asleep', k'ézhezh 'he's drinking (tea)', k'ezhézhen 'he who is drinking (tea)', k'ełch'ézhi 'blowfly', nuytelqúxch'q'u 'every day', tatghéshdneh 'I'll get tired', yiduch'ak'éłteł 'I smoke'. On the last the pitch rises slightly on each successive syllable, then rises sharply on -k'éł-, then falls sharply on -teł. There seem to be some exceptions to this rule, but apparently only in compounds, e.g. Láshk'aht'an 'Old Stony River Language' (Láshk'a-ht'an 'L.-people'). There are no phonemic (other than syntactic) stresses or pitches.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Dena'ina is not in the catalog. Of the three title-hits: Lovick & Tuttle 2012 (IJAL, discourse prosody) is closed-access; only the abstract was obtained (OpenAlex) and it concerns intonation units/pitch/pause, not word-stress placement — still the best candidate for a modern word-stress background section, priority high. Tuttle 2008 'Acoustic Correlates of Stress in the Inland Dialect of Dena'ina' is an ANLA paper item (TI000T2008, format non-digital, ca. 8 pp. presentation outline annotated by Kari) — print only, priority high (request scan from ANLA). Leer 1976 is a comparative Proto-Athabaskan tone-development manuscript, not about Dena'ina stress, not located, low priority. this search of works with stress in the title found and read three open sources beyond the list: Kari 1977 Dena'ina (Tanaina) Noun Dictionary (ERIC scan on archive.org) gives the only explicit first-hand stress rule — Upper Inlet stresses the stem syllable; Outer Inlet and Inland stress a full vowel (a,i,u) in the syllable before the stem/final syllable — proposed as the deciding statement; Lovick 2005 (KUPS) only notes the name Dena'ina is penult-stressed and that tone is not phonemic; Boraas 2010 grammar (via the Internet Archive; earlier listed as unreachable) is silent on stress. Kari 1975, Tenenbaum 1976 vol. 1 and Kalifornsky 1991 ERIC scans, qenaga.org pages and the archived Sava Stephan lessons were also a full-text search for stress/accent: no stress statement. Web search/OpenAlex/scholar.archive. All files and are in

The intonation pattern of Tanaina does include a simple [struck word] form of word-stress, however. new_statements.rule_in_words: Dena'ina has no tone. Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word regardless of morphological structure or vowel grade (in verbs this is the syllable before the stem); stress is not contrastive. The published dictionary statement (Kari 1977, Noun Dictionary introduction) gives the same pre-stem/penultimate stress for the Outer Inlet and Inland dialects, restricted there to full vowels (a, i, u), and says the Upper Inlet dialect instead always stresses the stem (final) syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Krauss describes the pitch contour of a long verb (pitch rises slightly on each successive syllable, then sharply on the stressed penult -k'éł-, then falls sharply on the final -teł).
new_statements.exceptions: Krauss: 'some exceptions to this rule, but apparently only in compounds', e.g. Láshk'aht'an with stress on the first syllable of the compound. Kari 1977 (Noun Dictionary intro, scan p. 27): 'The Dena'ina alphabet does not mark stress. There are differences in the way Dena'inas accentuate their words. The Upper Inlet people always stress the stem syllable, but in Outer Inlet and Inland full vowels (a, i, u) before the stem (or before the final syllable) are stressed.' Tenenbaum 1978: 27: reduced e 'rarely carries stress' (Krauss's examples k'ézhezh, tatghéshdneh nevertheless show stressed penult e). Holton & Mueller 2005 (catalogue description only): phrase-final evidential particles shift stress from pre-stem (penultimate) to stem (ultimate) syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (verbs and nouns cited in isolation), Inland (Nondalton-Lime Village) dialect data; Krauss frames stress as part of the 'intonation pattern' with only syntactic (phrase-level) stress/pitch beyond it. Dialect-dependent: Upper Inlet stem-final vs Outer Inlet/Inland pre-stem per Kari 1977.
new_statements.identity_note: Krauss 1973 describes the Inland (Nondalton-Lime Village) dialect, with earlier fieldwork on other Tanaina dialects; Tenenbaum 1978 is also Nondalton. Kari 1977 (Noun Dictionary, all dialects) reports a dialect split: Outer Inlet and Inland stress the full vowel before the stem/final syllable (penult), whereas Upper Inlet (Knik-Eklutna-Susitna; Tyonek per Kari's grouping) 'always stress[es] the stem syllable' (word-final in nouns). Boraas 2010 describes the Kenai (Outer Inlet) dialect and is silent on stress.

new_statements.reading: Dena'ina word stress is dialect-split: Upper Inlet stresses the stem (word-final) syllable; Outer Inlet and Inland stress a full vowel (a, i, u — i.e. not the reduced vowel e) in the syllable immediately before the stem/final syllable, so a weight-sensitive penultimate-type stress. Stress is not marked in the orthography. The four minimal pairs across dialects (IO vs U) illustrate the shift.

sources.citation: Kari, James (comp.). 1977. Dena'ina (Tanaina) Noun Dictionary. Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center (ERIC ED169768 microfiche scan on archive.org).
sources.quote: The Dena'ina alphabet does not mark stress. There are differences in the way Dena'inas accentuate their words. The Upper Inlet people always stress the stem syllable, but in Outer Inlet and Inland full vowels (a, i, u) before the stem (or before the final syllable) are stressed. Compare: snipe yuzizt (IO) / yuyiz (U); humpback salmon qughuna (IO) / qughuna (U); jaeger nuk'etvaq'i (IO) / nuk'etbaq'i (U); seal qutsaghit'iy (IO) / gqutsaghit'iy (U).
sources.locator: Introduction, dialect-pronunciation notes, pp. 26-27 of the ERIC scan (printed page number not in scanned)
sources.note: First-hand statement by the principal Dena'ina lexicographer: stress is not. Upper Inlet dialect stresses the (final) stem syllable; Outer Inlet and Inland dialects stress a full vowel (a, i, u) in the syllable before the stem/final syllable, i.e. a weight-sensitive stem-adjacent (penultimate) stress. Dialect-split system.

sources.citation: Lovick, Olga. 2005. Agentivity and Participant Marking in Dena'ina Athabascan: A Text-Based Study. PhD dissertation, Universität zu Köln (KUPS 1727).
sources.quote: Pronunciation of the name varies with the dialect: In the Inland dialects, the glottal stop is pronounced [dənʌʔɪnʌ], while it is left out in the Upper Inland dialect [dənʌ͡ɪnʌ]. In both cases, the penultimate syllable is stressed. ... Note that this inventory is very small, and many Proto-Athabascan distinctions such as quality, length, nasalization, or tone are not phonemic in Dena'ina.
sources.note: Only an incidental remark: the word Dena'ina is stressed on its penultimate syllable in both Inland and Upper Inlet; tone is not phonemic. No general stress rule given (phonology section is explicitly minimal).

sources.quote: We investigate the prosodic realization of discourse structure in Dena'ina based on two narratives. We assume that a Dena'ina text consists of informational and prosodic "building blocks" of different sizes that we call paragraphs, story units, intonation units, and prosodic words. ... we demonstrate that story units and intonation unit boundaries are cued by prosodic markers including pitch, rhyme length, and following pause.
sources.locator: abstract (OpenAlex record); full text closed at doi:10.1086/665671 (Unpaywall is_oa=false, OpenAlex closed, Semantic Scholar CLOSED; U Chicago and JSTOR pages blocked from here)
sources.note: The only modern, instrumental, peer-reviewed prosodic description; defines the prosodic word and its cues (pitch, rhyme length) and would supersede the 1973/1977 statements on stress placement.
